The truce reduced air strikes and ground offensives, partially reopened Sanaa airport, and improved fuel imports through Hudaydah port, producing measurable improvements in civilian life. However, the parties could not agree on the next phase of negotiations, and the truce expired in October 2022 without a permanent ceasefire agreement.

title: Abu Dhabi Houthi Drone Attack
description: The Houthi movement carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on Abu Dhabi, the UAE capital, in January 2022, killing three people and striking oil storage facilities near Abu Dhabi's international airport. The attack was the first Houthi strike on the UAE and reflected the group's expanded long-range attack capabilities and frustration with UAE involvement in the conflict. The Abu Dhabi attack temporarily increased UAE military activity in Yemen but also contributed to Abu Dhabi's eventual de-escalation with the Houthis.

title: Presidential Leadership Council Replaces Hadi Government
description: President Hadi resigned in April 2022 and transferred authority to a newly formed Presidential Leadership Council comprising eight members representing diverse factions of the anti-Houthi coalition. The council was brokered by Saudi Arabia as an attempt to create a more broadly legitimate governing body for government-controlled Yemen, replacing the discredited Hadi administration that had governed from exile in Riyadh for seven years. The PLC immediately struggled with internal divisions and the challenge of governing a fragmented territory.

title: Saudi-Iran Normalization and Yemen Peace Prospects
description: The surprise normalization agreement between Saudi Arabia and Iran brokered by China in March 2023 transformed the diplomatic landscape around the Yemen conflict, as the principal external backer of the Houthi movement and the leader of the anti-Houthi coalition reached an accommodation. Saudi Arabia launched direct negotiations with the Houthi movement on ending the war, offering significant concessions including payment of civil servant salaries and a political role for the Houthis in a transitional government. Cautious optimism emerged that a negotiated end to the conflict was possible for the first time since 2016.

title: Humanitarian Situation Remains Catastrophic Despite Reduced Fighting
description: Despite the reduction in large-scale military operations following the 2022 truce and the Saudi-Houthi negotiations, Yemen's humanitarian situation remained among the worst in the world. Over 21 million people — roughly two-thirds of the population — required humanitarian assistance, and 17 million faced food insecurity. Funding shortfalls at international humanitarian organizations meant that food rations were cut and medical programs suspended, leaving millions without life-sustaining assistance. A decade of war left over 150,000 direct conflict deaths, four million internally displaced people, and an economy producing less per capita than at independence in 1990.

title: Houthi Movement Consolidates Governance in Northern Yemen
description: The Houthi movement deepened its administrative control over northern Yemen in 2023, building parallel government institutions to replace those loyal to the internationally recognized government. The Houthis imposed taxes on businesses, controlled aid distribution, and ran an education system that incorporated their religious-political ideology. International organizations noted that the Houthi administration, while authoritarian, provided a degree of public order in some areas that had been absent since the collapse of central government in 2014.

title: Houthi Red Sea Attacks — Disrupting Global Shipping
description: Beginning in November 2023 and escalating through 2024, the Houthi movement launched dozens of attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea using anti-ship missiles, drones, and commandeered vessels, ostensibly in solidarity with Gaza following the October 7 Hamas attack and Israel's military response. The attacks severely disrupted global maritime trade, forcing major shipping lines to reroute vessels around the Cape of Good Hope and causing significant increases in shipping costs worldwide. The Red Sea crisis transformed the Houthis from a local actor into a significant force affecting global commerce, prompting the United States to redesignate Ansar Allah as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization.

title: US-UK Military Strikes on Houthi Infrastructure
description: The United States and United Kingdom launched extensive air and naval strikes against Houthi military infrastructure in Yemen beginning in January 2024, targeting missile launch sites, drone facilities, radar systems, and weapons storage to protect international shipping in the Red Sea. The strikes were the most significant direct Western military action in Yemen since the conflict began and represented a new front in an already complex war. The Houthis absorbed the strikes and continued attacking shipping, demonstrating their resilience and the limitations of air power against a decentralized guerrilla force.

title: Ceasefire Negotiations and Political Transition Discussions
description: Negotiations for a comprehensive ceasefire and political transition in Yemen continued in 2025, with UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg working to bridge the gap between the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council and the Houthi-controlled Supreme Political Council. Saudi Arabia's desire to extricate itself from the Yemen conflict and focus on Vision 2030 economic projects created new diplomatic momentum, with Riyadh accepting Houthi conditions that would have been unacceptable in earlier years. A formal end to the war remained elusive but progress in reducing large-scale military operations gave cautious grounds for optimism.

title: Southern Yemen — Separatist Aspirations Persist
description: The Southern Transitional Council maintained its de facto autonomous administration over much of southern Yemen in 2025, with Aden functioning as a separate capital and the STC's Security Belt Forces controlling the streets. Negotiations between the STC and the Presidential Leadership Council on integrating their institutions remained stalled, with the south's ultimate political status — autonomy within a federated Yemen or eventual independence — unresolved. The persistence of southern separatism ensured that any peace agreement ending the Houthi conflict would still leave Yemen's territorial integrity contested.
